This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and al-Nasa'i related from Buraydah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the ʿIsha' prayer ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and similar surahs." The hadith of Jabir in the Sahih has already been mentioned, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: "Why did you not pray with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾?" Al-Tabarani related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) instructed him to recite in the Fajr prayer ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to pray the two rakʿahs of ḍuḥa with their two surahs: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and ﴿By the morning brightness﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. Some have said that the oath by these things and similar ones mentioned before and those to come is by elision of a noun, meaning: "and by the Lord of the sun, and the Lord of the moon," and likewise for the rest. But there is no compulsion to this and no reason for it. His saying "and its brightness" (ḍuḥāhā) is a second oath. Mujahid said: "ḍuḥāhā" means its light and its radiance, and the brightness is attributed to the sun because it occurs when the sun rises high. Al-Kalbi also said this.

Qatadah said: "ḍuḥāhā" is all of its daytime.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḍuḥā is the daytime.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of al-ḍuḥā is the morning, which is the light of the sun.

Abu al-Haytham said: al-ḍuḥā is the opposite of shade; it is the light of the sun upon the face of the earth. Its origin is al-ḍuḥy, but they found the yā' heavy and changed it to an alif. It has been said: what is known among the Arabs is that al-ḍuḥā is when the sun has risen and a little after; when it extends further, it is al-ḍuḥā'  with a long vowel.

Al-Mubarrad said: al-ḍuḥā and al-ḍaḥwah are derived from al-ḍiḥḥ, which is light, and the alif and waw were substituted for the ḥā'.

There has been disagreement concerning what the answer to the oath is. It has been said that it is His saying ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam was omitted because the speech had grown long, so its length became a substitute for it. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, meaning: "By the sun... [you will be resurrected]," and likewise "you will surely be resurrected." It has been said that its implied sense is: "Allah will surely destroy the people of Mecca for their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as He destroyed Thamud because they denied Salih." As for ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, it is a statement following His saying ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ by way of digression, and it is not part of the answer to the oath at all. It has also been said that it is by inversion and reordering without elision, and the meaning is: "He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, and he has indeed failed who corrupts it. By the sun and its brightness." The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾: that is, it follows it, which happens when it rises after the sun sets. One says talā yatlū tulūwan when he follows.

The exegetes said: that occurs in the first half of the month: when the sun sets, the moon follows it in brightness and comes after it in light.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾: that is, it covers the sun, so it takes away its light, and the sun sets and the horizons grow dark. It has been said it covers the horizons, and it has been said the earth, though neither has been mentioned because that is known. The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾: "mā" may be a verbal noun, meaning "and by the heaven and its building"; and it may be relative, meaning "and by He who built it." The choice of "mā" over "man" is to intend the descriptive sense for the purpose of exaltation, as if he said: "and by the Mighty, Great in Majesty, who built it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred the first, and there is no basis for the saying of one who said that making it a verbal noun disrupts the composition. Ibn Jarir preferred the second.

*Jadhimah does not know who spread it out, nor who dwells on the lofty Throne.*

The first is preferable.

*Your heart went off among the beautiful, longing, after youth, when the time of gray hair came.*

ʿAṭāʾ said: it intends everything He created of jinn and humankind, and the indefinite form is for exaltation. It has been said the intended meaning is the self of Adam.

﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾: that is, He made it know and understand their two states and what is in them of good and evil.

Mujahid said: He made it know the path of wickedness and of piety, obedience and disobedience.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-alhamahā" means He made it know the path of good and the path of evil, as He said: ﴿and We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: when Allah intends good for His servant, He inspires him with good and he acts upon it; and when He intends evil for him, He inspires him with evil and he acts upon it.

Ibn Zayd said: He placed in it that by His granting it success to piety and His forsaking it to wickedness. Al-Zajjaj chose this and understood inspiration as granting success and forsaking.

Al-Wahidi said: this is the proper interpretation of inspiration, for clarifying, teaching and informing fall short of inspiration, and inspiration is that it is cast into his heart and placed within it; and when Allah casts something into the heart of His servant, He binds him to that thing.

He said: this is explicit that Allah created piety in the believer and wickedness in the disbeliever.

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾: that is, he has won who purifies his soul, makes it grow, and raises it high by piety, attaining every sought thing and gaining every beloved thing. We have already mentioned that this is the answer to the oath according to the preferred view. The root of zakāh is growth and increase, and from it: zakā al-zarʿ when the crop has increased.

The lexicographers said: "dassāhā" is originally "dassasahā", from al-tadsīs, which is concealing a thing within a thing. So the meaning of "dassāhā" in the verse is: he concealed it and made it obscure, and did not make it known through obedience and righteous deeds. The noble Arabs used to dwell in high places so that their place would become known and guests would seek them; and the base Arabs used to dwell in hills and low places so that their place would be hidden from visitors.

It has been said the meaning of "dassāhā" is: led it astray.

From this is the saying of the poet:

*You are the one who concealed ʿAmr, so his wives became widows, lost.*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "and he has indeed failed who corrupts it" means he slipped his soul into the company of the righteous while not being of them.

*Thamud denied in its transgression.* Ṭaghwā is a noun from transgression, which led them to denial, and transgression is exceeding the limit in sins; the bāʾ is causal.

It has been said: Thamud denied by its ṭaghwā, that is, by its punishment with which they were promised, and punishment was called ṭaghwā because it transgressed upon them; so the bāʾ on this view is for transitivity.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "bi-ṭaghwāhā" means with all of it.

The majority read "bi-ṭaghwāhā" with a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Hammad ibn Salamah read it with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ. On the first reading, it is a verbal noun in the sense of transgression, and the yāʾ and waw were changed only to distinguish the noun from the adjective, since they often change yāʾ in nouns, as in taqwā and sarwā. On the second reading it is a verbal noun like ruj‘ā and ḥusnā and similar; it has been said they are two dialects.

The meaning of "inbaʿatha" is that he undertook it and stood to do it; one says "baʿthtuhu ʿalā al-amr fa-inbaʿatha lahu," and this was explained previously in al-Aʿraf.

﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾, meaning Salih: ﴿"The she-camel of Allah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "she-camel of Allah" is in the accusative in the sense of "leave the she-camel of Allah."

Al-Farra' said: he warned them against it, and every warning is in the accusative. "And her drink" is conjoined to "she-camel", and it is her drinking of the water.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: Salih said to them: "Leave the she-camel of Allah, do not hamstring her, and leave her drink, which is her drinking from the stream; do not oppose her on the day of her drinking." So they denied his warning to them.

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: that is, the most wretched hamstrung her. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them because they approved of what he did. Qatadah said: he did not hamstring her until his young and old, male and female, all followed him.

Al-Farra' said: two hamstrung her, and the Arabs say "these two are the best of people" and "these two are the best of people," therefore it did not say "the most wretched of them" in the dual.

﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them﴾: that is, He destroyed them and enveloped them in punishment. The reality of "damdamah" is the intensifying and repeating of punishment; one says "dammamtu ʿalā al-shay'" meaning I covered it over, and "dammama ʿalayhi al-qabr" meaning it covered him, and "nāqah madmūmah" when fat has covered it. "Damdamah" is destruction by uprooting; so said al-Mu'arrij.

In al-Sihah it says: "dammamtu al-shay'" when you stick it to the ground and crush it, and "dammama Allah ʿalayhim" meaning He destroyed them.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "dammama" when he punished with complete punishment.

The pronoun in "fa-sawwāhā" refers to the dammamah: that is, He leveled the dammamah upon them and made it general over them, so it encompassed their young and old. It has been said it refers to the earth, meaning He leveled the earth over them and placed them under the dust. It has been said it refers to the community, namely Thamud.

Al-Farra' said: "sawwā al-ummah" means He sent punishment down upon its young and old, in the sense of "sawwā baynahum," making them equal.

The majority read "fa-dammama" with a mim between the two dals. Ibn al-Zubayr read "fa-dahdama" with a hā' between the two dals. Al-Qurtubi said: they are two dialects, as one says "imtaqaʿa lawnuhu" and "ihtaqaʿa lawnuhu."

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾: that is, Allah did that to them without fearing any consequence or any repercussion. The pronoun in "ʿuqbāhā" returns to the deed or to the dammamah implied by "dammama."

Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: the statement refers to the one who hamstrung her, not to Allah, glory be to Him: that is, the one who hamstrung her did not fear the outcome of what he did.

It has been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fear the consequence of the destruction of his people, nor did he dread any harm returning to him from their punishment, because he had warned them. The first view is preferable.

The majority read "wa-lā yakhāfu" with a waw, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fa'.

Al-Hakim related and graded sahih from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "wa-ḍuḥāhā" that he said: its light. "And the moon when it follows it": he said: it followed it. "And the day when it reveals it": he said: it lit it up. "And the heaven and He who built it": he said: Allah built the heaven and the earth. "And the earth and what spread it": he said: spread it. "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety": he said: He taught it obedience and disobedience.

He said: 'Rather, it is a matter that has already been decreed for them.' He said: 'Then why do they work?' He said: 'Whoever Allah has created for one of the two states, He facilitates him for its work. Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Imran ibn Husayn that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you see what people do today and strive at, is it a matter that has already been decreed for them and has passed in a destiny that has already preceded, or is it regarding what they face anew, which their Prophet has brought to them and by which you have established proof against them?' He said: 'Rather, it is a matter that has already been decreed for them.' He said: 'Then why do they work?' He said: 'Whoever Allah has created for one of the two states, He facilitates him for its work. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i related from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Allah, give my soul its righteousness, and purify it, You are the best of those who purify it. You are its Guardian and its Master.'"

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿And he has certainly failed who buries it﴾: he means, "he deceived it" (makar biha).

He said, "Yes." He said: "Two men: the little reddish one of Thamud who slaughtered the she-camel, and the one who strikes you on this [pointing to his horn] until this becomes wet from it." He meant his beard.

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. Some have said that the oath by these things and similar ones mentioned before and those to come is by elision of a noun, meaning: "and by the Lord of the sun, and the Lord of the moon," and likewise for the rest. But there is no compulsion to this and no reason for it. His saying "and its brightness" (ḍuḥāhā) is a second oath. Mujahid said: "ḍuḥāhā" means its light and its radiance, and the brightness is attributed to the sun because it occurs when the sun rises high. Al-Kalbi also said this.

Qatadah said: "ḍuḥāhā" is all of its daytime.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḍuḥā is the daytime.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of al-ḍuḥā is the morning, which is the light of the sun.

Abu al-Haytham said: al-ḍuḥā is the opposite of shade; it is the light of the sun upon the face of the earth. Its origin is al-ḍuḥy, but they found the yā' heavy and changed it to an alif. It has been said: what is known among the Arabs is that al-ḍuḥā is when the sun has risen and a little after; when it extends further, it is al-ḍuḥā'  with a long vowel.

Al-Mubarrad said: al-ḍuḥā and al-ḍaḥwah are derived from al-ḍiḥḥ, which is light, and the alif and waw were substituted for the ḥā'.

There has been disagreement concerning what the answer to the oath is. It has been said that it is His saying ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam was omitted because the speech had grown long, so its length became a substitute for it. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, meaning: "By the sun... [you will be resurrected]," and likewise "you will surely be resurrected." It has been said that its implied sense is: "Allah will surely destroy the people of Mecca for their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as He destroyed Thamud because they denied Salih." As for ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, it is a statement following His saying ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ by way of digression, and it is not part of the answer to the oath at all. It has also been said that it is by inversion and reordering without elision, and the meaning is: "He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, and he has indeed failed who corrupts it. By the sun and its brightness." The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾: that is, it follows it, which happens when it rises after the sun sets. One says talā yatlū tulūwan when he follows.

The exegetes said: that occurs in the first half of the month: when the sun sets, the moon follows it in brightness and comes after it in light.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾: that is, it covers the sun, so it takes away its light, and the sun sets and the horizons grow dark. It has been said it covers the horizons, and it has been said the earth, though neither has been mentioned because that is known. The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾: "mā" may be a verbal noun, meaning "and by the heaven and its building"; and it may be relative, meaning "and by He who built it." The choice of "mā" over "man" is to intend the descriptive sense for the purpose of exaltation, as if he said: "and by the Mighty, Great in Majesty, who built it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred the first, and there is no basis for the saying of one who said that making it a verbal noun disrupts the composition. Ibn Jarir preferred the second.

﴿And by the earth and He who spread it out﴾: the discussion of this "mā" is like the discussion of the one before it. The meaning of ṭaḥāhā is spread it, as the majority of exegetes said, as in His saying "daḥāhā" (spread it). They said: "ṭaḥāhā" and "daḥāhā" are one: that is, He spread it out from every side. Al-ṭaḥw is spreading. It has been said the meaning of ṭaḥāhā is He divided it, and it has been said He created it, and from this is the saying of the poet:

*Jadhimah does not know who spread it out, nor who dwells on the lofty Throne.*

The first is preferable.

Al-ṭaḥw also means departing. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: ṭaḥā al-rajul means he went off into the earth; one says "I do not know where he went off to," and one says "his heart went off with him," meaning it took him away. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Your heart went off among the beautiful, longing, after youth, when the time of gray hair came.*

﴿And by the soul and He who fashioned it﴾: the discussion of this "mā" is as previously mentioned. The meaning of sawwāhā is He created it, brought it into being, and formed its limbs.

ʿAṭāʾ said: it intends everything He created of jinn and humankind, and the indefinite form is for exaltation. It has been said the intended meaning is the self of Adam.

﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾: that is, He made it know and understand their two states and what is in them of good and evil.

Mujahid said: He made it know the path of wickedness and of piety, obedience and disobedience.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-alhamahā" means He made it know the path of good and the path of evil, as He said: ﴿and We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: when Allah intends good for His servant, He inspires him with good and he acts upon it; and when He intends evil for him, He inspires him with evil and he acts upon it.

Ibn Zayd said: He placed in it that by His granting it success to piety and His forsaking it to wickedness. Al-Zajjaj chose this and understood inspiration as granting success and forsaking.

Al-Wahidi said: this is the proper interpretation of inspiration, for clarifying, teaching and informing fall short of inspiration, and inspiration is that it is cast into his heart and placed within it; and when Allah casts something into the heart of His servant, He binds him to that thing.

He said: this is explicit that Allah created piety in the believer and wickedness in the disbeliever.

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾: that is, he has won who purifies his soul, makes it grow, and raises it high by piety, attaining every sought thing and gaining every beloved thing. We have already mentioned that this is the answer to the oath according to the preferred view. The root of zakāh is growth and increase, and from it: zakā al-zarʿ when the crop has increased.

﴿And he has indeed failed who corrupts it﴾: that is, he has lost who misguides it and leads it astray.

The lexicographers said: "dassāhā" is originally "dassasahā", from al-tadsīs, which is concealing a thing within a thing. So the meaning of "dassāhā" in the verse is: he concealed it and made it obscure, and did not make it known through obedience and righteous deeds. The noble Arabs used to dwell in high places so that their place would become known and guests would seek them; and the base Arabs used to dwell in hills and low places so that their place would be hidden from visitors.

It has been said the meaning of "dassāhā" is: led it astray.

From this is the saying of the poet:

*You are the one who concealed ʿAmr, so his wives became widows, lost.*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "and he has indeed failed who corrupts it" means he slipped his soul into the company of the righteous while not being of them.

*Thamud denied in its transgression.* Ṭaghwā is a noun from transgression, which led them to denial, and transgression is exceeding the limit in sins; the bāʾ is causal.

It has been said: Thamud denied by its ṭaghwā, that is, by its punishment with which they were promised, and punishment was called ṭaghwā because it transgressed upon them; so the bāʾ on this view is for transitivity.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "bi-ṭaghwāhā" means with all of it.

The majority read "bi-ṭaghwāhā" with a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Hammad ibn Salamah read it with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ. On the first reading, it is a verbal noun in the sense of transgression, and the yāʾ and waw were changed only to distinguish the noun from the adjective, since they often change yāʾ in nouns, as in taqwā and sarwā. On the second reading it is a verbal noun like ruj‘ā and ḥusnā and similar; it has been said they are two dialects.

﴿When the most wretched of them rose up﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is "kadhdhabat" or "bi-ṭaghwāhā": that is, when the most wretched of Thamud arose, and he was Qidar ibn Salif, who hamstrung the she-camel. The meaning of "inbaʿatha" is that he undertook it and stood to do it; one says "baʿthtuhu ʿalā al-amr fa-inbaʿatha lahu," and this was explained previously in al-Aʿraf.

﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾, meaning Salih: ﴿"The she-camel of Allah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "she-camel of Allah" is in the accusative in the sense of "leave the she-camel of Allah."

Al-Farra' said: he warned them against it, and every warning is in the accusative. "And her drink" is conjoined to "she-camel", and it is her drinking of the water.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: Salih said to them: "Leave the she-camel of Allah, do not hamstring her, and leave her drink, which is her drinking from the stream; do not oppose her on the day of her drinking." So they denied his warning to them.

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: that is, the most wretched hamstrung her. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them because they approved of what he did. Qatadah said: he did not hamstring her until his young and old, male and female, all followed him.

Al-Farra' said: two hamstrung her, and the Arabs say "these two are the best of people" and "these two are the best of people," therefore it did not say "the most wretched of them" in the dual.

﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them﴾: that is, He destroyed them and enveloped them in punishment. The reality of "damdamah" is the intensifying and repeating of punishment; one says "dammamtu ʿalā al-shay'" meaning I covered it over, and "dammama ʿalayhi al-qabr" meaning it covered him, and "nāqah madmūmah" when fat has covered it. "Damdamah" is destruction by uprooting; so said al-Mu'arrij.

In al-Sihah it says: "dammamtu al-shay'" when you stick it to the ground and crush it, and "dammama Allah ʿalayhim" meaning He destroyed them.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "dammama" when he punished with complete punishment.

The pronoun in "fa-sawwāhā" refers to the dammamah: that is, He leveled the dammamah upon them and made it general over them, so it encompassed their young and old. It has been said it refers to the earth, meaning He leveled the earth over them and placed them under the dust. It has been said it refers to the community, namely Thamud.

Al-Farra' said: "sawwā al-ummah" means He sent punishment down upon its young and old, in the sense of "sawwā baynahum," making them equal.

The majority read "fa-dammama" with a mim between the two dals. Ibn al-Zubayr read "fa-dahdama" with a hā' between the two dals. Al-Qurtubi said: they are two dialects, as one says "imtaqaʿa lawnuhu" and "ihtaqaʿa lawnuhu."

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾: that is, Allah did that to them without fearing any consequence or any repercussion. The pronoun in "ʿuqbāhā" returns to the deed or to the dammamah implied by "dammama."

Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: the statement refers to the one who hamstrung her, not to Allah, glory be to Him: that is, the one who hamstrung her did not fear the outcome of what he did.

It has been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fear the consequence of the destruction of his people, nor did he dread any harm returning to him from their punishment, because he had warned them. The first view is preferable.

The majority read "wa-lā yakhāfu" with a waw, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fa'.

"And the day when it reveals it": he said: it lit it up. "And the heaven and He who built it": he said: Allah built the heaven and the earth. "And the earth and what spread it": he said: spread it. "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety": he said: He taught it obedience and disobedience.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾: that is, it covers the sun, so it takes away its light, and the sun sets and the horizons grow dark. It has been said it covers the horizons, and it has been said the earth, though neither has been mentioned because that is known. The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾: "mā" may be a verbal noun, meaning "and by the heaven and its building"; and it may be relative, meaning "and by He who built it." The first is preferable.

ʿAṭāʾ said: it intends everything He created of jinn and humankind, and the indefinite form is for exaltation. It has been said the intended meaning is the self of Adam.

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

Juwaybir is weak.

Ibn Jarir also related from him, regarding ﴿with its rebellion﴾: he said, "The name of the punishment that came to it is al-Taghwa (the rebellion/punishment). So He said: ﴿Thamud denied with its punishment﴾."

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) instructed him to recite in the Fajr prayer ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. Some have said that the oath by these things and similar ones mentioned before and those to come is by elision of a noun, meaning: "and by the Lord of the sun, and the Lord of the moon," and likewise for the rest. But there is no compulsion to this and no reason for it. His saying "and its brightness" (ḍuḥāhā) is a second oath. Mujahid said: "ḍuḥāhā" means its light and its radiance, and the brightness is attributed to the sun because it occurs when the sun rises high. Al-Kalbi also said this.

Qatadah said: "ḍuḥāhā" is all of its daytime.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḍuḥā is the daytime.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of al-ḍuḥā is the morning, which is the light of the sun.

Abu al-Haytham said: al-ḍuḥā is the opposite of shade; it is the light of the sun upon the face of the earth. Its origin is al-ḍuḥy, but they found the yā' heavy and changed it to an alif. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam was omitted because the speech had grown long, so its length became a substitute for it. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, meaning: "By the sun... [you will be resurrected]," and likewise "you will surely be resurrected." By the sun and its brightness." The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾: that is, it follows it, which happens when it rises after the sun sets. One says talā yatlū tulūwan when he follows.

The exegetes said: that occurs in the first half of the month: when the sun sets, the moon follows it in brightness and comes after it in light.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾: that is, it covers the sun, so it takes away its light, and the sun sets and the horizons grow dark. It has been said it covers the horizons, and it has been said the earth, though neither has been mentioned because that is known. The first view is preferable.

The first is preferable.

Al-Wahidi said: this is the proper interpretation of inspiration, for clarifying, teaching and informing fall short of inspiration, and inspiration is that it is cast into his heart and placed within it; and when Allah casts something into the heart of His servant, He binds him to that thing.

He said: this is explicit that Allah created piety in the believer and wickedness in the disbeliever.

So the meaning of "dassāhā" in the verse is: he concealed it and made it obscure, and did not make it known through obedience and righteous deeds. The noble Arabs used to dwell in high places so that their place would become known and guests would seek them; and the base Arabs used to dwell in hills and low places so that their place would be hidden from visitors.

It has been said the meaning of "dassāhā" is: led it astray.

From this is the saying of the poet:

*You are the one who concealed ʿAmr, so his wives became widows, lost.*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "and he has indeed failed who corrupts it" means he slipped his soul into the company of the righteous while not being of them.

*Thamud denied in its transgression.* Ṭaghwā is a noun from transgression, which led them to denial, and transgression is exceeding the limit in sins; the bāʾ is causal.

It has been said: Thamud denied by its ṭaghwā, that is, by its punishment with which they were promised, and punishment was called ṭaghwā because it transgressed upon them; so the bāʾ on this view is for transitivity.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "bi-ṭaghwāhā" means with all of it.

On the first reading, it is a verbal noun in the sense of transgression, and the yāʾ and waw were changed only to distinguish the noun from the adjective, since they often change yāʾ in nouns, as in taqwā and sarwā. On the second reading it is a verbal noun like ruj‘ā and ḥusnā and similar; it has been said they are two dialects.

The meaning of "inbaʿatha" is that he undertook it and stood to do it; one says "baʿthtuhu ʿalā al-amr fa-inbaʿatha lahu," and this was explained previously in al-Aʿraf.

﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾, meaning Salih: ﴿"The she-camel of Allah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "she-camel of Allah" is in the accusative in the sense of "leave the she-camel of Allah."

Al-Farra' said: he warned them against it, and every warning is in the accusative. "And her drink" is conjoined to "she-camel", and it is her drinking of the water.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: Salih said to them: "Leave the she-camel of Allah, do not hamstring her, and leave her drink, which is her drinking from the stream; do not oppose her on the day of her drinking." So they denied his warning to them.

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: that is, the most wretched hamstrung her. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them because they approved of what he did. Qatadah said: he did not hamstring her until his young and old, male and female, all followed him.

Al-Farra' said: two hamstrung her, and the Arabs say "these two are the best of people" and "these two are the best of people," therefore it did not say "the most wretched of them" in the dual.

﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them﴾: that is, He destroyed them and enveloped them in punishment. In al-Sihah it says: "dammamtu al-shay'" when you stick it to the ground and crush it, and "dammama Allah ʿalayhim" meaning He destroyed them.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "dammama" when he punished with complete punishment.

The pronoun in "fa-sawwāhā" refers to the dammamah: that is, He leveled the dammamah upon them and made it general over them, so it encompassed their young and old. It has been said it refers to the earth, meaning He leveled the earth over them and placed them under the dust. It has been said it refers to the community, namely Thamud.

Al-Farra' said: "sawwā al-ummah" means He sent punishment down upon its young and old, in the sense of "sawwā baynahum," making them equal.

The majority read "fa-dammama" with a mim between the two dals. Ibn al-Zubayr read "fa-dahdama" with a hā' between the two dals. Al-Qurtubi said: they are two dialects, as one says "imtaqaʿa lawnuhu" and "ihtaqaʿa lawnuhu."

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾: that is, Allah did that to them without fearing any consequence or any repercussion. The pronoun in "ʿuqbāhā" returns to the deed or to the dammamah implied by "dammama."

Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: the statement refers to the one who hamstrung her, not to Allah, glory be to Him: that is, the one who hamstrung her did not fear the outcome of what he did.

It has been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fear the consequence of the destruction of his people, nor did he dread any harm returning to him from their punishment, because he had warned them. The first view is preferable.

The majority read "wa-lā yakhāfu" with a waw, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fa'.

Al-Hakim related and graded sahih from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "wa-ḍuḥāhā" that he said: its light. "And the moon when it follows it": he said: it followed it. "And the day when it reveals it": he said: it lit it up. "And the heaven and He who built it": he said: Allah built the heaven and the earth. "And the earth and what spread it": he said: spread it. "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety": he said: He taught it obedience and disobedience.

He said: 'Rather, it is a matter that has already been decreed for them.' He said: 'Then why do they work?' He said: 'Whoever Allah has created for one of the two states, He facilitates him for its work. Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

He meant his beard.

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

He said: 'Whoever Allah has created for one of the two states, He facilitates him for its work. And the confirmation of this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾.'" And something similar to this hadith will come in the surah that follows this one.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i related from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Allah, give my soul its righteousness, and purify it, You are the best of those who purify it. You are its Guardian and its Master.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related it from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and added: "When he recited this verse ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, he would say: [the supplication] and he added: 'And he was in prayer.'"

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿And he has certainly failed who buries it﴾: he means, "he deceived it" (makar biha).

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related through the chain of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say regarding His saying ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾, the verse: 'A soul has succeeded whom Allah has purified, and a soul has failed whom Allah has made to fail from every good.'" Juwaybir is weak.

Ibn Jarir also related from him, regarding ﴿with its rebellion﴾: he said, "The name of the punishment that came to it is al-Taghwa (the rebellion/punishment). So He said: ﴿Thamud denied with its punishment﴾."

He said: 'A mighty, powerful, unassailable man arose for it among his people, like Abu Zam'ah.'"

He meant his beard.

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. Some have said that the oath by these things and similar ones mentioned before and those to come is by elision of a noun, meaning: "and by the Lord of the sun, and the Lord of the moon," and likewise for the rest. But there is no compulsion to this and no reason for it. His saying "and its brightness" (ḍuḥāhā) is a second oath. Mujahid said: "ḍuḥāhā" means its light and its radiance, and the brightness is attributed to the sun because it occurs when the sun rises high. Al-Kalbi also said this.

Qatadah said: "ḍuḥāhā" is all of its daytime.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḍuḥā is the daytime.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of al-ḍuḥā is the morning, which is the light of the sun.

Abu al-Haytham said: al-ḍuḥā is the opposite of shade; it is the light of the sun upon the face of the earth. Its origin is al-ḍuḥy, but they found the yā' heavy and changed it to an alif. It has been said: what is known among the Arabs is that al-ḍuḥā is when the sun has risen and a little after; when it extends further, it is al-ḍuḥā'  with a long vowel.

Al-Mubarrad said: al-ḍuḥā and al-ḍaḥwah are derived from al-ḍiḥḥ, which is light, and the alif and waw were substituted for the ḥā'.

There has been disagreement concerning what the answer to the oath is. It has been said that it is His saying ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam was omitted because the speech had grown long, so its length became a substitute for it. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, meaning: "By the sun... [you will be resurrected]," and likewise "you will surely be resurrected." It has been said that its implied sense is: "Allah will surely destroy the people of Mecca for their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as He destroyed Thamud because they denied Salih." As for ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, it is a statement following His saying ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ by way of digression, and it is not part of the answer to the oath at all. It has also been said that it is by inversion and reordering without elision, and the meaning is: "He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, and he has indeed failed who corrupts it. By the sun and its brightness." The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾: that is, it follows it, which happens when it rises after the sun sets. One says talā yatlū tulūwan when he follows.

The exegetes said: that occurs in the first half of the month: when the sun sets, the moon follows it in brightness and comes after it in light.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾: that is, it covers the sun, so it takes away its light, and the sun sets and the horizons grow dark. It has been said it covers the horizons, and it has been said the earth, though neither has been mentioned because that is known. The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾: "mā" may be a verbal noun, meaning "and by the heaven and its building"; and it may be relative, meaning "and by He who built it." The choice of "mā" over "man" is to intend the descriptive sense for the purpose of exaltation, as if he said: "and by the Mighty, Great in Majesty, who built it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred the first, and there is no basis for the saying of one who said that making it a verbal noun disrupts the composition. Ibn Jarir preferred the second.

﴿And by the earth and He who spread it out﴾: the discussion of this "mā" is like the discussion of the one before it. The meaning of ṭaḥāhā is spread it, as the majority of exegetes said, as in His saying "daḥāhā" (spread it). They said: "ṭaḥāhā" and "daḥāhā" are one: that is, He spread it out from every side. Al-ṭaḥw is spreading. It has been said the meaning of ṭaḥāhā is He divided it, and it has been said He created it, and from this is the saying of the poet:

*Jadhimah does not know who spread it out, nor who dwells on the lofty Throne.*

The first is preferable.

Al-ṭaḥw also means departing. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: ṭaḥā al-rajul means he went off into the earth; one says "I do not know where he went off to," and one says "his heart went off with him," meaning it took him away. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Your heart went off among the beautiful, longing, after youth, when the time of gray hair came.*

﴿And by the soul and He who fashioned it﴾: the discussion of this "mā" is as previously mentioned. The meaning of sawwāhā is He created it, brought it into being, and formed its limbs.

ʿAṭāʾ said: it intends everything He created of jinn and humankind, and the indefinite form is for exaltation. It has been said the intended meaning is the self of Adam.

﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾: that is, He made it know and understand their two states and what is in them of good and evil.

Mujahid said: He made it know the path of wickedness and of piety, obedience and disobedience.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-alhamahā" means He made it know the path of good and the path of evil, as He said: ﴿and We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: when Allah intends good for His servant, He inspires him with good and he acts upon it; and when He intends evil for him, He inspires him with evil and he acts upon it.

Ibn Zayd said: He placed in it that by His granting it success to piety and His forsaking it to wickedness. Al-Zajjaj chose this and understood inspiration as granting success and forsaking.

Al-Wahidi said: this is the proper interpretation of inspiration, for clarifying, teaching and informing fall short of inspiration, and inspiration is that it is cast into his heart and placed within it; and when Allah casts something into the heart of His servant, He binds him to that thing.

He said: this is explicit that Allah created piety in the believer and wickedness in the disbeliever.

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾: that is, he has won who purifies his soul, makes it grow, and raises it high by piety, attaining every sought thing and gaining every beloved thing. We have already mentioned that this is the answer to the oath according to the preferred view. The root of zakāh is growth and increase, and from it: zakā al-zarʿ when the crop has increased.

﴿And he has indeed failed who corrupts it﴾: that is, he has lost who misguides it and leads it astray.

The lexicographers said: "dassāhā" is originally "dassasahā", from al-tadsīs, which is concealing a thing within a thing. So the meaning of "dassāhā" in the verse is: he concealed it and made it obscure, and did not make it known through obedience and righteous deeds. The noble Arabs used to dwell in high places so that their place would become known and guests would seek them; and the base Arabs used to dwell in hills and low places so that their place would be hidden from visitors.

It has been said the meaning of "dassāhā" is: led it astray.

From this is the saying of the poet:

*You are the one who concealed ʿAmr, so his wives became widows, lost.*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "and he has indeed failed who corrupts it" means he slipped his soul into the company of the righteous while not being of them.

*Thamud denied in its transgression.* Ṭaghwā is a noun from transgression, which led them to denial, and transgression is exceeding the limit in sins; the bāʾ is causal.

It has been said: Thamud denied by its ṭaghwā, that is, by its punishment with which they were promised, and punishment was called ṭaghwā because it transgressed upon them; so the bāʾ on this view is for transitivity.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "bi-ṭaghwāhā" means with all of it.

The majority read "bi-ṭaghwāhā" with a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Hammad ibn Salamah read it with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ. On the first reading, it is a verbal noun in the sense of transgression, and the yāʾ and waw were changed only to distinguish the noun from the adjective, since they often change yāʾ in nouns, as in taqwā and sarwā. On the second reading it is a verbal noun like ruj‘ā and ḥusnā and similar; it has been said they are two dialects.

﴿When the most wretched of them rose up﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is "kadhdhabat" or "bi-ṭaghwāhā": that is, when the most wretched of Thamud arose, and he was Qidar ibn Salif, who hamstrung the she-camel. The meaning of "inbaʿatha" is that he undertook it and stood to do it; one says "baʿthtuhu ʿalā al-amr fa-inbaʿatha lahu," and this was explained previously in al-Aʿraf.

﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾, meaning Salih: ﴿"The she-camel of Allah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "she-camel of Allah" is in the accusative in the sense of "leave the she-camel of Allah."

Al-Farra' said: he warned them against it, and every warning is in the accusative. "And her drink" is conjoined to "she-camel", and it is her drinking of the water.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: Salih said to them: "Leave the she-camel of Allah, do not hamstring her, and leave her drink, which is her drinking from the stream; do not oppose her on the day of her drinking." So they denied his warning to them.

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: that is, the most wretched hamstrung her. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them because they approved of what he did. Qatadah said: he did not hamstring her until his young and old, male and female, all followed him.

Al-Farra' said: two hamstrung her, and the Arabs say "these two are the best of people" and "these two are the best of people," therefore it did not say "the most wretched of them" in the dual.

﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them﴾: that is, He destroyed them and enveloped them in punishment. The reality of "damdamah" is the intensifying and repeating of punishment; one says "dammamtu ʿalā al-shay'" meaning I covered it over, and "dammama ʿalayhi al-qabr" meaning it covered him, and "nāqah madmūmah" when fat has covered it. "Damdamah" is destruction by uprooting; so said al-Mu'arrij.

In al-Sihah it says: "dammamtu al-shay'" when you stick it to the ground and crush it, and "dammama Allah ʿalayhim" meaning He destroyed them.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "dammama" when he punished with complete punishment.

The pronoun in "fa-sawwāhā" refers to the dammamah: that is, He leveled the dammamah upon them and made it general over them, so it encompassed their young and old. It has been said it refers to the earth, meaning He leveled the earth over them and placed them under the dust. It has been said it refers to the community, namely Thamud.

Al-Farra' said: "sawwā al-ummah" means He sent punishment down upon its young and old, in the sense of "sawwā baynahum," making them equal.

The majority read "fa-dammama" with a mim between the two dals. Ibn al-Zubayr read "fa-dahdama" with a hā' between the two dals. Al-Qurtubi said: they are two dialects, as one says "imtaqaʿa lawnuhu" and "ihtaqaʿa lawnuhu."

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾: that is, Allah did that to them without fearing any consequence or any repercussion. The pronoun in "ʿuqbāhā" returns to the deed or to the dammamah implied by "dammama."

Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: the statement refers to the one who hamstrung her, not to Allah, glory be to Him: that is, the one who hamstrung her did not fear the outcome of what he did.

It has been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fear the consequence of the destruction of his people, nor did he dread any harm returning to him from their punishment, because he had warned them. The first view is preferable.

The majority read "wa-lā yakhāfu" with a waw, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fa'.

"And the day when it reveals it": he said: it lit it up. "And the heaven and He who built it": he said: Allah built the heaven and the earth. "And the earth and what spread it": he said: spread it. "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety": he said: He taught it obedience and disobedience.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. The exegetes said: that occurs in the first half of the month: when the sun sets, the moon follows it in brightness and comes after it in light.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

He said: this is explicit that Allah created piety in the believer and wickedness in the disbeliever.

It has been said the meaning of "dassāhā" is: led it astray.

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) instructed him to recite in the Fajr prayer ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to pray the two rakʿahs of ḍuḥa with their two surahs: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ and ﴿By the morning brightness﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. Some have said that the oath by these things and similar ones mentioned before and those to come is by elision of a noun, meaning: "and by the Lord of the sun, and the Lord of the moon," and likewise for the rest. But there is no compulsion to this and no reason for it. His saying "and its brightness" (ḍuḥāhā) is a second oath. Mujahid said: "ḍuḥāhā" means its light and its radiance, and the brightness is attributed to the sun because it occurs when the sun rises high. Al-Kalbi also said this.

Qatadah said: "ḍuḥāhā" is all of its daytime.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḍuḥā is the daytime.

Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of al-ḍuḥā is the morning, which is the light of the sun.

Abu al-Haytham said: al-ḍuḥā is the opposite of shade; it is the light of the sun upon the face of the earth. Its origin is al-ḍuḥy, but they found the yā' heavy and changed it to an alif. It has been said: what is known among the Arabs is that al-ḍuḥā is when the sun has risen and a little after; when it extends further, it is al-ḍuḥā'  with a long vowel.

Al-Mubarrad said: al-ḍuḥā and al-ḍaḥwah are derived from al-ḍiḥḥ, which is light, and the alif and waw were substituted for the ḥā'.

There has been disagreement concerning what the answer to the oath is. It has been said that it is His saying ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam was omitted because the speech had grown long, so its length became a substitute for it. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, meaning: "By the sun... [you will be resurrected]," and likewise "you will surely be resurrected." It has been said that its implied sense is: "Allah will surely destroy the people of Mecca for their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as He destroyed Thamud because they denied Salih." As for ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, it is a statement following His saying ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾ by way of digression, and it is not part of the answer to the oath at all. It has also been said that it is by inversion and reordering without elision, and the meaning is: "He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, and he has indeed failed who corrupts it. By the sun and its brightness." The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾: that is, it follows it, which happens when it rises after the sun sets. One says talā yatlū tulūwan when he follows.

The exegetes said: that occurs in the first half of the month: when the sun sets, the moon follows it in brightness and comes after it in light.

Al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes full, so it follows the sun in illumination and light, meaning that when its light is complete it becomes a follower of the sun in giving light, that is, it is like it in brightness, and that is on the bright nights.

It has been said: when its rising follows the rising of the sun.

Qatadah said: that is the night of the crescent when the crescent sets.

Ibn Zayd said: when the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting. Al-Farra' said: talāhā means it took from it, meaning the moon takes from the light of the sun.

﴿And by the day when it reveals it﴾: that is, it reveals the sun, because when the day spreads the sun becomes fully manifest, as if it revealed it, even though it is the one that spreads the day.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, meaning it reveals the darkness, though no mention of darkness has preceded, because the meaning is known. Al-Farra' said: like your saying "our morning became cold," meaning our morning became cold. The first view is preferable.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a side of her showed, and she withheld the other side.*

It has been said that the meaning is: it revealed what is on the earth of living creatures and others after it had been hidden in the night. It has been said it revealed the world, and it has been said it revealed the earth.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾: that is, it covers the sun, so it takes away its light, and the sun sets and the horizons grow dark. It has been said it covers the horizons, and it has been said the earth, though neither has been mentioned because that is known. The first view is preferable.

﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾: "mā" may be a verbal noun, meaning "and by the heaven and its building"; and it may be relative, meaning "and by He who built it." The choice of "mā" over "man" is to intend the descriptive sense for the purpose of exaltation, as if he said: "and by the Mighty, Great in Majesty, who built it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred the first, and there is no basis for the saying of one who said that making it a verbal noun disrupts the composition. Ibn Jarir preferred the second.

﴿And by the earth and He who spread it out﴾: the discussion of this "mā" is like the discussion of the one before it. The meaning of ṭaḥāhā is spread it, as the majority of exegetes said, as in His saying "daḥāhā" (spread it). They said: "ṭaḥāhā" and "daḥāhā" are one: that is, He spread it out from every side. Al-ṭaḥw is spreading. It has been said the meaning of ṭaḥāhā is He divided it, and it has been said He created it, and from this is the saying of the poet:

*Jadhimah does not know who spread it out, nor who dwells on the lofty Throne.*

The first is preferable.

Al-ṭaḥw also means departing. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: ṭaḥā al-rajul means he went off into the earth; one says "I do not know where he went off to," and one says "his heart went off with him," meaning it took him away. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Your heart went off among the beautiful, longing, after youth, when the time of gray hair came.*

﴿And by the soul and He who fashioned it﴾: the discussion of this "mā" is as previously mentioned. The meaning of sawwāhā is He created it, brought it into being, and formed its limbs.

ʿAṭāʾ said: it intends everything He created of jinn and humankind, and the indefinite form is for exaltation. It has been said the intended meaning is the self of Adam.

﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾: that is, He made it know and understand their two states and what is in them of good and evil.

Mujahid said: He made it know the path of wickedness and of piety, obedience and disobedience.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-alhamahā" means He made it know the path of good and the path of evil, as He said: ﴿and We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: when Allah intends good for His servant, He inspires him with good and he acts upon it; and when He intends evil for him, He inspires him with evil and he acts upon it.

Ibn Zayd said: He placed in it that by His granting it success to piety and His forsaking it to wickedness. Al-Zajjaj chose this and understood inspiration as granting success and forsaking.

Al-Wahidi said: this is the proper interpretation of inspiration, for clarifying, teaching and informing fall short of inspiration, and inspiration is that it is cast into his heart and placed within it; and when Allah casts something into the heart of His servant, He binds him to that thing.

He said: this is explicit that Allah created piety in the believer and wickedness in the disbeliever.

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾: that is, he has won who purifies his soul, makes it grow, and raises it high by piety, attaining every sought thing and gaining every beloved thing. We have already mentioned that this is the answer to the oath according to the preferred view. The root of zakāh is growth and increase, and from it: zakā al-zarʿ when the crop has increased.

﴿And he has indeed failed who corrupts it﴾: that is, he has lost who misguides it and leads it astray.

The lexicographers said: "dassāhā" is originally "dassasahā", from al-tadsīs, which is concealing a thing within a thing. So the meaning of "dassāhā" in the verse is: he concealed it and made it obscure, and did not make it known through obedience and righteous deeds. The noble Arabs used to dwell in high places so that their place would become known and guests would seek them; and the base Arabs used to dwell in hills and low places so that their place would be hidden from visitors.

It has been said the meaning of "dassāhā" is: led it astray.

From this is the saying of the poet:

*You are the one who concealed ʿAmr, so his wives became widows, lost.*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "and he has indeed failed who corrupts it" means he slipped his soul into the company of the righteous while not being of them.

*Thamud denied in its transgression.* Ṭaghwā is a noun from transgression, which led them to denial, and transgression is exceeding the limit in sins; the bāʾ is causal.

It has been said: Thamud denied by its ṭaghwā, that is, by its punishment with which they were promised, and punishment was called ṭaghwā because it transgressed upon them; so the bāʾ on this view is for transitivity.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: "bi-ṭaghwāhā" means with all of it.

The majority read "bi-ṭaghwāhā" with a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Hammad ibn Salamah read it with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ. On the first reading, it is a verbal noun in the sense of transgression, and the yāʾ and waw were changed only to distinguish the noun from the adjective, since they often change yāʾ in nouns, as in taqwā and sarwā. On the second reading it is a verbal noun like ruj‘ā and ḥusnā and similar; it has been said they are two dialects.

﴿When the most wretched of them rose up﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is "kadhdhabat" or "bi-ṭaghwāhā": that is, when the most wretched of Thamud arose, and he was Qidar ibn Salif, who hamstrung the she-camel. The meaning of "inbaʿatha" is that he undertook it and stood to do it; one says "baʿthtuhu ʿalā al-amr fa-inbaʿatha lahu," and this was explained previously in al-Aʿraf.

﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾, meaning Salih: ﴿"The she-camel of Allah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "she-camel of Allah" is in the accusative in the sense of "leave the she-camel of Allah."

Al-Farra' said: he warned them against it, and every warning is in the accusative. "And her drink" is conjoined to "she-camel", and it is her drinking of the water.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: Salih said to them: "Leave the she-camel of Allah, do not hamstring her, and leave her drink, which is her drinking from the stream; do not oppose her on the day of her drinking." So they denied his warning to them.

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: that is, the most wretched hamstrung her. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them because they approved of what he did. Qatadah said: he did not hamstring her until his young and old, male and female, all followed him.

Al-Farra' said: two hamstrung her, and the Arabs say "these two are the best of people" and "these two are the best of people," therefore it did not say "the most wretched of them" in the dual.

﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them﴾: that is, He destroyed them and enveloped them in punishment. The reality of "damdamah" is the intensifying and repeating of punishment; one says "dammamtu ʿalā al-shay'" meaning I covered it over, and "dammama ʿalayhi al-qabr" meaning it covered him, and "nāqah madmūmah" when fat has covered it. "Damdamah" is destruction by uprooting; so said al-Mu'arrij.

In al-Sihah it says: "dammamtu al-shay'" when you stick it to the ground and crush it, and "dammama Allah ʿalayhim" meaning He destroyed them.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "dammama" when he punished with complete punishment.

The pronoun in "fa-sawwāhā" refers to the dammamah: that is, He leveled the dammamah upon them and made it general over them, so it encompassed their young and old. It has been said it refers to the earth, meaning He leveled the earth over them and placed them under the dust. It has been said it refers to the community, namely Thamud.

Al-Farra' said: "sawwā al-ummah" means He sent punishment down upon its young and old, in the sense of "sawwā baynahum," making them equal.

The majority read "fa-dammama" with a mim between the two dals. Ibn al-Zubayr read "fa-dahdama" with a hā' between the two dals. Al-Qurtubi said: they are two dialects, as one says "imtaqaʿa lawnuhu" and "ihtaqaʿa lawnuhu."

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾: that is, Allah did that to them without fearing any consequence or any repercussion. The pronoun in "ʿuqbāhā" returns to the deed or to the dammamah implied by "dammama."

Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: the statement refers to the one who hamstrung her, not to Allah, glory be to Him: that is, the one who hamstrung her did not fear the outcome of what he did.

It has been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not fear the consequence of the destruction of his people, nor did he dread any harm returning to him from their punishment, because he had warned them. The first view is preferable.

The majority read "wa-lā yakhāfu" with a waw, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fa'.

Al-Hakim related and graded sahih from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "wa-ḍuḥāhā" that he said: its light. "And the moon when it follows it": he said: it followed it. "And the day when it reveals it": he said: it lit it up. "And the heaven and He who built it": he said: Allah built the heaven and the earth. "And the earth and what spread it": he said: spread it. "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety": he said: He taught it obedience and disobedience.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 91, verse 1–15 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding ﴿And the earth and He who spread it out﴾: he said, "He divided it (qassamaha)." ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾: he said, "From good and evil."

Al-Hakim related, and authenticated it, also from him regarding ﴿and inspired it﴾: he said, "He made it necessary for it, its wickedness and its righteousness."

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Imran ibn Husayn that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you see what people do today and strive at, is it a matter that has already been decreed for them and has passed in a destiny that has already preceded, or is it regarding what they face anew, which their Prophet has brought to them and by which you have established proof against them?' He said: 'Rather, it is a matter that has already been decreed for them.' He said: 'Then why do they work?' He said: 'Whoever Allah has created for one of the two states, He facilitates him for its work. And the confirmation of this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾.'" And something similar to this hadith will come in the surah that follows this one.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i related from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Allah, give my soul its righteousness, and purify it, You are the best of those who purify it. You are its Guardian and its Master.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related it from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and added: "When he recited this verse ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, he would say: [the supplication] and he added: 'And he was in prayer.'"

Muslim also related the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam.

Ahmad related something similar from the hadith of Aishah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾: he said, "He has certainly succeeded whose soul Allah has purified." ﴿And he has certainly failed who buries it﴾: he said, "He has certainly failed whose soul Allah has buried, so that He misguided it." ﴿And he will not fear its consequence﴾: he said, "He will not fear any retribution from anyone."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿And he has certainly failed who buries it﴾: he means, "he deceived it" (makar biha).

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related through the chain of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say regarding His saying ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾, the verse: 'A soul has succeeded whom Allah has purified, and a soul has failed whom Allah has made to fail from every good.'" Juwaybir is weak.

Ibn Jarir also related from him, regarding ﴿with its rebellion﴾: he said, "The name of the punishment that came to it is al-Taghwa (the rebellion/punishment). So He said: ﴿Thamud denied with its punishment﴾."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abd Allah ibn Zam'ah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon, and mentioned the she-camel and the one who slaughtered her, and said: ﴿When the most wretched of them was sent forth﴾. He said: 'A mighty, powerful, unassailable man arose for it among his people, like Abu Zam'ah.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il related from Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ali: "Shall I tell you about the most wretched of people?" He said, "Yes." He said: "Two men: the little reddish one of Thamud who slaughtered the she-camel, and the one who strikes you on this [pointing to his horn] until this becomes wet from it." He meant his beard.
